title: Weaving the World Wide Web
summary: A scientist at a giant physics lab in Switzerland was tired of losing information. So he invented a way to link pages together with clickable words, and called it the World Wide Web. Then his lab gave it away to the whole world for free.

sections.heading: The Road and the Shops
paragraphs: Before we meet the inventor of the Web, we need to clear up one of the most common mix-ups in all of technology. Many people use the words 'Internet' and 'Web' as if they mean the same thing. They do not.

Think of the Internet as a giant system of roads, motorways and delivery vans that stretches around the planet. Its job is to carry packets from one computer to another, using the TCP/IP rules you met in Parts 6 to 8. The roads do not care what is inside the vans. A van might be carrying an email, a video call, a game move, a file or a web page.

The World Wide Web is one of the things that travel along those roads. It is like a huge collection of shops, libraries and noticeboards along the roadside, all with signposts pointing to each other. The Web is made of pages that are linked together, and you look at them using a program called a browser. Email is not the Web. Online games are not usually the Web. Most of the apps on a phone use the Internet without being the Web at all.

The timing makes this clear. As the Computer History Museum points out, the Internet's roots lie in the United States in the late 1960s, while the Web was invented about 20 years later by an Englishman working in Switzerland. By the time the Web appeared, the Internet already connected hundreds of thousands of computers. People were already sending email, posting on Usenet and copying files. What they did not have was an easy way to find, link and read information spread across all those machines.

So in this part we are not watching the Internet being born. We are watching someone build a brilliant new service on top of it, one so popular that, for many people, it became the face of the whole Internet.

sections.heading: Dreams of Linked Words
paragraphs: The idea of jumping from one piece of information to another is much older than the Web. In Part 2 you met Vannevar Bush, who in 1945 imagined the Memex, a desk where a reader could build 'trails' connecting one document to another on microfilm. It was never built, but it inspired generations of computer scientists.

In the 1960s an American thinker named Ted Nelson took the idea further. He coined the word 'hypertext', and he presented it at a computing conference in 1965. Hyper means 'beyond', so hypertext is text that goes beyond the page: words that link to other words, documents that connect to other documents. Nelson dreamed of a worldwide system called Project Xanadu, a vast library in which every document could be linked to every other, quotes would always link back to their original source, and authors would be paid tiny amounts whenever their work was read. Xanadu was extremely ambitious, and although Nelson worked on it for decades, it was never finished in the form he imagined.

Meanwhile, at Brown University in 1967, Andries van Dam and his colleagues built one of the first working hypertext systems, the Hypertext Editing System, which ran on an IBM computer. But the most famous early demonstration came from Douglas Engelbart and his team at the Stanford Research Institute, the same SRI that later received the first ARPANET message.

Picture the scene. It is 9 December 1968, at a computer conference in the Civic Auditorium in San Francisco. Somewhere between 1,000 and 2,000 people pack the hall (accounts differ). Engelbart sits at a special console, wearing a headset, while behind him a huge screen shows what his computer is doing. The computer itself is not even in the room. It is back at SRI, about 30 miles away, connected by borrowed telephone lines and microwave links. For about 90 minutes, Engelbart shows things nobody in the audience has seen before: a pointing device he calls a 'mouse', text that can be edited on screen, words that are links you can click to jump to other information, and colleagues back at SRI appearing on screen and working on the same document with him. At the end the crowd gives him a standing ovation. People later called it 'the Mother of All Demos'.

Almost twenty years later, hypertext reached ordinary computer owners. In August 1987 Apple released HyperCard, created by the programmer Bill Atkinson, and gave it away with every new Macintosh computer. HyperCard let people build 'stacks' of cards with pictures, text and buttons. Clicking a button could take you to another card. Teachers made lessons with it, children made games with it, and the famous adventure game Myst was first built using it. But HyperCard stacks lived on one computer. You could not click a button in your stack and jump to a card on a computer in another country.

So by the late 1980s there were two great inventions sitting side by side. Hypertext could link information beautifully, but only inside one machine or one system. The Internet could connect millions of machines, but had no easy way to link their information together. Someone needed to marry the two.

sections.heading: A Lab Full of Lost Information
paragraphs: That someone was working at CERN, the European Organization for Nuclear Research, just outside Geneva, with parts of the laboratory in Switzerland and parts in France. CERN was founded in 1954 so that European countries could do big physics experiments together that none of them could afford alone. Its scientists study the tiniest particles of matter by smashing them together in giant machines called particle accelerators. In 1989 CERN finished a new accelerator called LEP, which ran around a circular tunnel 27 kilometres long, deep underground.

Thousands of physicists, engineers and students from dozens of countries worked on experiments at CERN, and many of them stayed only for a few years. They brought every kind of computer you can imagine, each with its own operating system, its own way of storing files and its own programs. If you wanted to know how a piece of equipment worked, or who had written a certain program, you might have to log in to several different computers, learn several different systems, or simply wander the corridors asking people.

Tim Berners-Lee knew this problem well. He was born in London in 1955. His parents, Mary Lee Woods and Conway Berners-Lee, were mathematicians who had both worked on one of the earliest commercial computers, the Ferranti Mark 1. He studied physics at the University of Oxford, graduating in 1976, and while he was a student he built his own computer using parts that included an old television set.

In 1980 Berners-Lee spent about six months at CERN as a consultant writing software. To help himself keep track of all the people, programs and projects, he wrote a little program called Enquire. Its full name, 'Enquire Within Upon Everything', came from an old Victorian book of household advice he remembered from his childhood. In Enquire, every piece of information was a 'node', and nodes could be linked to each other, with labels describing how they were connected. Enquire was a hypertext system, but it ran on only one computer, and when he left CERN it was lost.

Berners-Lee returned to CERN in 1984 on a fellowship, this time to stay for years. The problem had not gone away. If anything, it was getting worse, because CERN was preparing for its biggest experiments yet. He realised that what CERN needed was not one central database that everyone had to fit into. CERN was too messy and too free for that. It needed a system that could link information wherever it already lived, on any computer, using the Internet that was already starting to connect CERN to the world.

sections.heading: Vague but Exciting
paragraphs: In March 1989 Berners-Lee wrote down his idea and handed it around CERN. The document had a plain, rather boring title: 'Information Management: A Proposal'. Inside, though, was something revolutionary.

He began by describing the problem. CERN was, he wrote, like a constantly changing web of people and projects, and information was always being lost. Because many people only stayed for about two years, newcomers wasted time working out who knew what, and details of old projects sometimes had to be rediscovered by detective work. He explained why tree-shaped systems, like folders inside folders or the topics of Usenet newsgroups, could not show all the different ways that things were connected. Real information, he argued, looked less like a tree and more like a web.

His answer was a system of 'nodes' and 'links'. A node could be anything: a document, a person, a piece of equipment, a project. Links would connect them. Crucially, the information would not need to be moved into one big new database. The system would be split into two parts: 'servers' that store information, and 'clients', programs on people's own computers that fetch and display it. That way, any kind of computer could join in. Special 'gateways' could even show existing information, such as phone directories and Usenet news, as hypertext, so the system would be useful from day one. At this stage he did not even have a proper name for it. The proposal mentions that it was being called 'Mesh'.

Berners-Lee gave the proposal to his boss, Mike Sendall. Sendall read it and wrote three words at the top of the first page: 'Vague but exciting...' It was not an official 'yes', and CERN did not create a big project for it. CERN was a physics lab, after all, not a software company. But Sendall quietly gave Berners-Lee room to keep working on the idea.

In September 1990 Sendall approved buying a new computer: a NeXT cube, a sleek black machine made by NeXT, the company Steve Jobs had started after leaving Apple. The NeXT had powerful tools that made it quicker to build programs with windows, menus and buttons. Sendall suggested that Berners-Lee could try out the NeXT by building his hypertext system on it. It was a clever way of saying 'go ahead' without needing permission from anyone higher up.

Berners-Lee also needed a name. According to his own account, he considered names such as 'Mine of Information', and 'The Information Mine', but rejected the second because its initials spelled TIM, which seemed a bit too much about himself. In the end he chose 'World Wide Web'. Some colleagues worried it was a mouthful, especially as 'WWW' takes longer to say out loud than the words themselves. But he liked the picture it created: a web of information spreading across the whole world.

sections.heading: Robert Cailliau and the Small Team
paragraphs: The Web was not a one-man show. Robert Cailliau was a Belgian engineer, born in 1947, who had worked at CERN since 1974. He had been thinking about hypertext himself, and when he heard about Berners-Lee's plans, he became the project's most enthusiastic supporter.

In November 1990 the two of them wrote a new, sharper version of the proposal called 'WorldWideWeb: Proposal for a HyperText Project'. It set out a plan to build the system in a few months with a small team. Cailliau was skilled at something Berners-Lee needed: persuading people, finding money, recruiting helpers and explaining the idea to managers who were busy with physics. He also later worked on a browser for Apple Macintosh computers, and in May 1994 he organised the very first international World Wide Web conference, held at CERN. The press nicknamed it the 'Woodstock of the Web', after a famous music festival.

Another key helper was Nicola Pellow, a mathematics student from England who came to CERN on a work placement. Berners-Lee's own browser ran only on the expensive NeXT computer, which very few people owned. So Pellow wrote a 'line-mode browser', a simple program that showed web pages as plain text on almost any computer terminal. Instead of clicking on links, you typed a number shown beside each link. It was not pretty, but it meant that almost anyone with access to an Internet-connected computer could use the Web straight away. In many ways it was just as important as the fancy NeXT version.

Other CERN colleagues joined in too. Jean-François Groff helped write code, and the team turned parts of the system into a shared library of programs that others could use to build their own browsers and servers. That decision, to make the pieces easy to reuse, helped the Web spread far beyond CERN.

This is a good moment to remember one of the rules of this story: do not let anyone tell you that Tim Berners-Lee invented the Internet. He did not, and he has always said so. He invented the World Wide Web, building on the Internet that hundreds of other people had created over the previous twenty years, and he built it with help from people like Cailliau and Pellow.

sections.heading: Three Simple Building Blocks
paragraphs: What made the Web work was not one giant invention but three simple ideas that fit together like the pieces of a plug and socket. You still use all three every single time you open a web page.

The first is HTML, which stands for HyperText Markup Language. It is the language web pages are written in. HTML uses short labels called tags to mark up text: this part is a heading, this part is a paragraph, this word is a link. Berners-Lee based it on a system called SGML that CERN already used for documents, so it looked familiar to people there. The very first version of HTML had only a small number of tags. A browser reads the HTML and decides how to show it on the screen, which is why the same page can appear on a giant monitor or a tiny phone.

The second is HTTP, the HyperText Transfer Protocol. Remember that a protocol is an agreed set of rules. HTTP describes the conversation between a browser and a web server. In its simplest early form it was almost like a polite note: the browser connects to the server and says, in effect, 'GET me this page, please', and the server sends the page back and hangs up. Because HTTP is so simple, it was easy for anyone to write a server or a browser that could talk to everyone else's.

The third is the URL, the Uniform Resource Locator, which is the address of a page. Berners-Lee first called it a Universal Document Identifier, and the general idea is now called a URI. A URL packs together everything a browser needs to know. Take the address of the first web page: http://info.cern.ch/hypertext/WWW/TheProject.html. The 'http' part says which protocol to use. 'info.cern.ch' is the name of the computer, which the Domain Name System from Part 8 turns into an IP address. The rest, '/hypertext/WWW/TheProject.html', says which file on that computer you want.

The genius was in what the system did not need. There was no central list of all pages and no need to ask permission to add a link. Anyone could put up a server, write a page and link to any other page on any other server in the world. A link could even point to a page that did not exist any more. Earlier hypertext dreamers, such as Ted Nelson, had wanted links that could never break. Berners-Lee accepted broken links as the price of letting the Web grow freely, without anyone in charge. That trade-off is the reason you sometimes see a 'page not found' message today, and it is also a big reason the Web grew so fast.

sections.heading: The First Website Goes Live
paragraphs: By late 1990 the pieces were working. On his NeXT computer, Berners-Lee had written the first web browser, which he called WorldWideWeb (later renamed Nexus to avoid confusion with the Web itself). It was not just a browser but also an editor: you could write and change pages and create links right there on screen, a bit like a modern word processor. The same NeXT machine also ran the first web server, at first called nxoc01.cern.ch and later known as info.cern.ch. By Christmas 1990 both the NeXT browser-editor and the line-mode browser could be demonstrated.

Because that one NeXT cube was the entire Web's first server, switching it off would have made the Web disappear. So a handwritten label was stuck on the computer, warning that the machine was a server and must not be powered down. That NeXT computer, label and all, has been kept as a treasured piece of history.

The first web page lived at info.cern.ch. It explained what the World Wide Web project was, how to get a browser, how to set up a server and who was working on it. In other words, the first website was about the Web itself, a sort of instruction manual and welcome sign rolled into one. You can still visit a copy of it today at info.cern.ch, and even try a simulator that shows how it looked in the old line-mode browser.

In March 1991 the line-mode browser was released to a limited group of people, and over the following months the Web was made available more widely at CERN. Then came the moment the outside world found out. On 6 August 1991 Berners-Lee posted a short summary of the WorldWideWeb project on alt.hypertext, a Usenet newsgroup for people interested in hypertext, and told readers where they could download the software for free. He posted to several other newsgroups around the same time. It was not a grand press launch. It was a message on a discussion board, the same kind of place you read about in Part 9.

Slowly, people began to try it. In December 1991 Paul Kunz, a physicist at the Stanford Linear Accelerator Center (SLAC) in California, set up the first web server outside Europe. SLAC used it to make its huge database of physics research papers searchable through the Web, which gave physicists a real reason to use it. In 1992 and early 1993, new graphical browsers appeared for different kinds of computers, with names like Erwise, ViolaWWW and Midas. a CERN browser for the Macintosh, MacWWW, built by Cailliau with help from Pellow, appeared around the end of 1992, and in February 1993 a team at the National Center for Supercomputing Applications in Illinois released a test version of a browser called Mosaic, which you will meet properly in Part 11.

sections.heading: A Gift to the Whole World
paragraphs: By early 1993 the Web was catching on, but there was a worry hanging over it. Who owned it? CERN had paid for its development. Could CERN one day start charging people to use the software, or demand fees from anyone who built a browser? Some other information systems of the time were starting to talk about licence fees, and companies were nervous about building on something that might suddenly cost money.

Berners-Lee and Cailliau pushed CERN's management to settle the question for good. On 30 April 1993 CERN signed a short document putting the World Wide Web software into the public domain. It declared that anyone could use, copy and change the Web's technology freely, with no fees payable to CERN. Later, CERN also released the software under an open licence to make sure it stayed free.

That decision may be one of the most generous gifts in the history of technology. Because nobody had to pay or ask permission, students, companies, schools, governments and hobbyists all over the world could build web servers and browsers and write pages. The Web did not belong to one company; it belonged to everyone who used it. Berners-Lee chose not to patent his invention or get rich from it.

In 1994 Berners-Lee left CERN for the Massachusetts Institute of Technology in the United States, where he founded the World Wide Web Consortium, or W3C, a group that brings together companies and experts to agree on open Web standards, so that pages work in every browser. He was later knighted, becoming Sir Tim Berners-Lee, and he received the Turing Award for 2016, often called the Nobel Prize of computing, the same honour Vint Cerf and Bob Kahn had received for 2004. In 2013 he shared the first Queen Elizabeth Prize for Engineering with Cerf, Kahn, Louis Pouzin and Marc Andreessen, a fitting reminder that the Internet and the Web were built by many hands.

Yet in 1993 the Web was still tiny. Even by the end of that year there were only a few hundred websites in the whole world, many of them at universities and physics labs. Most pages were plain grey screens of text and blue underlined links, with few or no pictures. To see them, many people still had to type commands into a line-mode browser or own an unusual computer. The Web had been woven, and it had been given away. Now it was waiting for a browser that would make it easy, colourful and fun enough for everyone.

deepDive: Why did the Web succeed when earlier, more sophisticated hypertext systems did not? Historians and computer scientists usually point to a set of deliberate simplifications. Ted Nelson's Xanadu called for two-way links that could never break, version tracking of every document and built-in micropayments for authors. Those features were powerful but required tight central coordination. Berners-Lee chose one-way links stored inside the page that makes them, which meant nobody had to keep a master index or ask permission to link. The cost was 'link rot': links that lead nowhere when a page moves or vanishes, the familiar 404 error. Academic hypertext researchers at the 1991 Hypertext conference were reportedly unimpressed by how simple the system was, yet that simplicity let it scale. A second reason is that the Web reused what already existed. It ran on TCP/IP, used the Domain Name System for computer names, borrowed its markup style from SGML, and included gateways to older systems such as FTP and Usenet, so early users found useful material immediately. The client-server split meant browsers could be written for any machine, and Nicola Pellow's line-mode browser made the Web reachable from cheap terminals long before graphical browsers spread. A third reason is licensing. In 1993 the University of Minnesota signalled that it might charge some users of its Gopher server software, and around the same time CERN declared the Web technology free; many historians see this contrast as one factor in the Web's rapid rise, though the arrival of the graphical Mosaic browser mattered too. There are also debates about credit. Berners-Lee is rightly called the inventor of the Web, but his own accounts stress the roles of Cailliau, Pellow, Groff and others, and the long line of hypertext pioneers from Bush and Nelson to Engelbart and van Dam. Finally, the original proposal shows something often forgotten: the Web was designed as a read-write medium. The first browser was also an editor, and Berners-Lee has said he always hoped people would create and edit pages as easily as they read them, an idea that later returned with blogs and wikis.
funFact: The very first web browser, called WorldWideWeb, was also a web page editor, so from the very beginning the Web was meant for writing pages as well as reading them.
